before: The division between mesons and baryons is actually based on their observed decay modes and is not strictly associated with their masses. <term id="import-auto-id1169737819849">Mesons</term> are hadrons that can decay to leptons and leave no hadrons, which implies that mesons are not conserved in number. <term id="import-auto-id1169737804482">Baryons</term> are hadrons that always decay to another baryon.
after: The distinction between these groups reflects their internal structure, which we will discuss later in this section, rather than their masses. Their observed decay patterns helped physicists recognize the distinction. <term id="import-auto-id1169737819849">Mesons</term> can decay entirely into particles that are not hadrons, so the number of mesons need not be conserved. In observed decays of unstable <term id="import-auto-id1169737804482">baryons</term>, the products include another baryon. These patterns illustrate the conservation rule introduced below.
